investmentReturn.metaDescription: Work out the real annual return (XIRR) on an investment with money paid in and taken out on different dates, see it next to the simple return, and replay the same money in an index you choose. Free, no signup.
investmentReturn.title: What did your investment really return?
investmentReturn.intro: Add every amount you put in or took out, with its date, and what it is worth now. You get the annual return Excel's XIRR would give — the figure to compare with a savings rate or an index.
investmentReturn.flowsHelp: One row per deposit or withdrawal, in any order.
investmentReturn.pasteHelp: Two columns, date then amount — copy them straight from Excel, Google Sheets or a bank export. Dates as 2024-01-31 or 31/01/2024 (day first). A minus sign means money taken out. Header and total lines are skipped.
investmentReturn.pasteAdded: Added {count, plural, one {# row} other {# rows}}.
investmentReturn.pasteSkipped: {count, plural, one {# line was} other {# lines were}} skipped: no date and amount found.
investmentReturn.pasteNone: No lines with a date and an amount were found.
investmentReturn.compareHelp: Replays your deposits and withdrawals, on the same dates, in an index or fund you choose. Nothing is picked for you.
investmentReturn.compareOtherPlaceholder: e.g. VWRL.L, or a company name
investmentReturn.empty: Add the amounts you put in, with their dates, and what the investment is worth now.
investmentReturn.kpiGainSub: Value plus money taken out, less money put in
investmentReturn.kpiMultipleSub: {currency}{x} back or still invested for every {currency}1 put in
investmentReturn.explain: The simple return counts every {currency} the same however long it was invested. The annual return weights each deposit by the time it was at work — money added last month has had no time to grow — so it is the figure to compare with a savings rate or an index.
investmentReturn.shortPeriod: Less than a year: an annual rate stretches the period out to twelve months, so it can look much bigger or smaller than the actual change ({simple} so far).
investmentReturn.noRate: No annual rate fits these figures.
investmentReturn.chartTitle: Money in and what it is worth
investmentReturn.diffAbove: Your annual return is ▲ {points} percentage points a year above it.
investmentReturn.diffBelow: Your annual return is ▼ {points} percentage points a year below it.
investmentReturn.diffSame: Your annual return is the same as its.
investmentReturn.compareNote: Each deposit buys, and each withdrawal sells, at the close on or before its date. Index prices leave out dividends, so a fund that reinvests them would be worth more.
investmentReturn.compareNoteFx: {from} prices converted to {to} at each day's exchange rate.
investmentReturn.compareSource: Prices: Yahoo Finance, delayed. Past returns say nothing about future ones.
investmentReturn.compareTooShort: The {name} price history here starts on {date}, after your first deposit, so it can't be compared.
investmentReturn.compareTooLarge: On {date} you took out more than the same money in {name} would have been worth then, so it can't be compared.
investmentReturn.compareFailed: Couldn't load prices for {name}. Try again later, or pick another.
investmentReturn.compareFxFailed: Couldn't load the {from} to {to} exchange rate, so the comparison is left out.
investmentReturn.copyLink: Copy a link to these figures
investmentReturn.privacy: Worked out in your browser — nothing you type is stored. The link carries your figures, so share it only with people you'd show them to.

problem.no_flows: Add at least one amount you put in, with its date.
problem.bad_date: One of the dates isn't a real date.
problem.bad_amount: One of the amounts isn't a number.
problem.bad_value: Enter what the investment is worth now (zero or more).
problem.after_value_date: One row is dated after the value date. Move it, or change the value date.
problem.no_money_in: Add at least one amount you put in.
problem.future: The value date can't be in the future.
problem.same_day: Your first deposit is on the value date: there has been no time for a return yet.

how: The annual return is the rate at which all your deposits and withdrawals, plus today's value, net to zero once each is discounted for the time since the first one — the same calculation as XIRR in Excel and Google Sheets, with 365-day years.
The simple return is the gain divided by everything you put in. It ignores timing, so it flatters money invested for years and understates money that went in recently.
Fees, taxes and inflation are not taken off unless they are already in your figures.

lifePlan.metaTitle: Life Plan — Your Money Year by Year, With a Home, Kids and Retirement
lifePlan.metaDescription: Put life events on a timeline — buying a home, a baby, a career break, retirement — and see your savings, debts and net worth year by year. Compare Plan A with Plan B. Free, no signup, nothing stored.
lifePlan.title: Can we afford it — and when?
lifePlan.intro: Add what you have today and the big things ahead: a home, a baby, a career break, retirement. See your money year by year, the dates that matter, and Plan A next to Plan B.
lifePlan.addPlanBHelp: Plan B starts as a copy of Plan A. Change anything — buy two years later, go part-time, rent instead.
lifePlan.todaysMoneyHelp: Takes inflation out, so a figure in 2045 reads like money today.
lifePlan.eventsHelp: Amounts in today's money; they grow with inflation to the year they happen.
lifePlan.eventsEmpty: No events yet. Add the big things ahead.

kindHint.oneOff: A wedding, a car, a big trip
kindHint.recurring: School fees, caring for a parent

f.sellCurrent: Sell the home I own first
f.incomeDropPct: Pay drop in the first year
f.changeHelp: +20 a promotion, −40 part-time, −100 a career break.

lifePlan.assumptionsHelp: Your assumptions, not forecasts. Change them and watch the plan move.
lifePlan.withdrawalHelp: For the financial-independence date: the share of savings you could draw each year.
lifePlan.milestonesEmpty: Nothing to flag in these years.

m.cashOut: Savings run out in {year} — something has to give.
m.depositShort: {year} home: you'd need {needed} for the deposit and costs, and you'd have {have}.
m.depositReady: Ready by {year} if nothing else changes.
m.independent: Financially independent in {year}: savings could cover your costs at the withdrawal rate.

lifePlan.compareTitle: Plan A and Plan B side by side
lifePlan.copyLink: Copy a link to this plan
lifePlan.privacy: Worked out in your browser — nothing is stored. The link carries your plan, so your partner can open it and edit their own copy.
how: Each year, take-home pay (grown at your pay-growth rate) less living costs, rent or mortgage, debt payments and that year's events goes into savings, which grow at your return. Homes grow at the house-price rate.
Amounts you type are in today's money and rise with inflation to the year they happen. Mortgages are repaid monthly, like the loan calculator.
There is no tax on savings, no pensions other than the income you set at retirement, and no selling of homes unless you choose it. It's a plan to think with, not a forecast or advice.
lifePlan.afterHorizon: After the years shown (to {year}) — make the plan longer to see it.

companyPlanner.noteTaxRate: Effective rate applied to pre-tax profit
companyPlanner.chartPLWaterfallSub: Revenue through to Net Profit — each bar shows the running total
companyPlanner.insightEBITDANeg: ⚠️ EBITDA is negative ({currency}{loss} loss). Review your cost structure — OpEx of {currency}{opex} exceeds Gross Profit of {currency}{grossProfit}.
companyPlanner.insightEBITDAHealthy: ✅ Healthy EBITDA margin of {margin}%. Businesses with margins above 15% typically command premium acquisition multiples.
companyPlanner.insightEBITDALow: 🟡 EBITDA margin of {margin}% — positive but below the 15% threshold where buyers typically apply higher multiples. Consider where costs can be optimised.
companyPlanner.insightEBITDAPosNetLoss: 🟡 EBITDA is positive but the business is loss-making after interest and tax. High interest costs or D&A may be suppressing reported profitability.
companyPlanner.chartWCBreakdownSub: Based on your AR / AP / Inventory days and revenue
companyPlanner.chartCFBridgeSub: Operating CF, CapEx drag, debt repayments and net position
companyPlanner.insightFCFNeg: ⚠️ Negative Free Cash Flow of {currency}{amount}. The business is consuming cash after CapEx. Review capital allocation or reduce CapEx spend.
companyPlanner.insightCashConvLow: 🟡 Cash conversion of {pct}% — below the 70–80% range that buyers expect. High working capital or CapEx relative to EBITDA drags cash quality.
companyPlanner.insightCashConvStrong: ✅ Strong cash conversion of {pct}%. Good FCF quality is a key driver of acquisition multiples.
companyPlanner.insightNegEquity: ⚠️ Negative book equity of {currency}{amount}. Total liabilities exceed total assets. This will complicate any sale or refinancing process and requires immediate attention.
companyPlanner.insightLeverageHigh: ⚠️ Leverage of {lev}× is above 3×. This is the typical ceiling for PE-backed acquisitions. Reducing debt would significantly improve exit options.
companyPlanner.insightLeverageGood: ✅ Leverage of {lev}× EBITDA — a conservative capital structure that keeps all exit options open, including PE and trade sale.
companyPlanner.insightLeverageAmber: 🟡 Leverage of {lev}× — approaching the upper end of what most buyers consider manageable. Monitor closely and prioritise debt reduction ahead of any exit.
companyPlanner.noteDCFFCF: FCF grows at 5% p.a. for 5 years in this model.
companyPlanner.exitValueCreated: Value created above book equity: {amount} ({mult}× book value)
companyPlanner.chartValuationSub: Equity value (after net debt) for each method
companyPlanner.insightNegEBITDAValuation: ⚠️ Negative EBITDA means the EV/EBITDA multiple cannot be applied. Focus on reaching EBITDA breakeven before targeting a sale.
companyPlanner.insightBlendedValuation: ℹ️ Multiples used are illustrative — actual market multiples vary significantly by sector, growth rate and deal size. The blended figure ({currency}{amount}) is a starting reference for exit planning, not a formal valuation.
companyPlanner.tradeSaleWhen: Best when EBITDA > 0 and revenue > {currency}500k. Strategic buyers pay synergy-adjusted premiums.
tradeSaleTips: Clean up financials 18–24 months before engaging advisors
Normalise EBITDA — add back owner salary above market rate, one-off costs
Run a competitive process with 3+ strategic buyers to drive price tension
companyPlanner.peBuyoutWhen: Best when EBITDA > {currency}500k, margin > 15%, leverage < 3×. PE needs debt capacity to fund the deal.
peBuyoutTips: Build a management team that can operate without the founder post-close
Demonstrate recurring revenue and low customer churn (NRR > 100% is ideal)
Maintain a 3-year financial track record with clean audit or review
Simplify the cap table — PE hates complex structures with multiple share classes
companyPlanner.mboWhen: Suitable at any size if management has appetite. Works best when FCF is strong enough to service acquisition debt.
mboTips: Arrange debt financing early — typically 3–4× EBITDA from specialist lenders
Align management incentives with EBITDA growth targets via equity ratchets
Keep lender covenants achievable — model a downside case before committing
Engage a specialist MBO solicitor and a deal structuring advisor from day one
companyPlanner.organicGrowthWhen: Always applicable. Reinvesting FCF rather than exiting — builds value ahead of a future sale at higher multiples.
organicGrowthTips: Reinvest FCF into highest-ROI activities — new markets, products or key hires
Manage working capital tightly — every day of AR reduction frees cash
Target 20%+ EBITDA margin before scaling headcount significantly
Build recurring revenue streams — subscription or retainer models command 2–3× higher multiples
companyPlanner.keyActionsTitle: Key Actions to Maximise Exit Price
companyPlanner.actionImproveMargin: Focus on margin improvement — buyers pay premium multiples for EBITDA margins above 15–20%. Review every cost line before entering a process.
companyPlanner.actionReduceDebt: Reduce debt before exit — leverage above 3× EBITDA compresses equity value and makes PE debt financing harder. Target sub-2× for maximum proceeds.
companyPlanner.actionImproveCashConversion: Improve cash conversion — buyers scrutinise the gap between EBITDA and free cash flow. Tighten AR collections and review CapEx spend.
companyPlanner.actionRecapitalise: Recapitalise the balance sheet — negative equity will complicate any sale, refinancing or due diligence process. Address before engaging advisors.
companyPlanner.actionCleanFinancials: Maintain 3 years of clean, audited (or reviewed) financials — this is the single most important factor in a smooth exit process.
companyPlanner.actionDocumentContracts: Document all customer contracts and revenue recognition — recurring, contracted revenue commands the highest multiples in any sale process.
companyPlanner.disclaimerText: This tool is for illustrative and planning purposes only. The valuations and insights above are indicative estimates based on simplified models. They do not constitute financial advice, a formal valuation or an offer to buy or sell any business. Consult a qualified M&A advisor, corporate finance professional or accountant before making any decisions related to a business sale, acquisition or restructuring.

mcp.whatIsBody: Connectors (built on an open standard called MCP) let an AI assistant use outside tools. With FinancePlots connected, Claude works the numbers out with the same formulas as this site instead of estimating them, and tells you which tool it used.
notes: Free, with no account or key.
The connector doesn’t save your questions or the numbers you send.
Figures are for learning and planning, not investment advice. The screener filters by your criteria; it never ranks or recommends shares.

takeHomeChat.askMode: Do you know your yearly salary, or how much you want to take home each month?
takeHomeChat.modeTarget: I know what I want to take home
takeHomeChat.askSalary: What is your salary per year, before tax?
takeHomeChat.askTarget: How much do you want to take home each month, after tax?
takeHomeChat.askRegion: Where do you pay income tax?
takeHomeChat.askPension: What percentage of your salary do you pay into your pension? Say 0 if none.
takeHomeChat.askPensionMethod: How is your pension paid? Your payslip or HR can tell you.
takeHomeChat.askLoan: Are you repaying a student loan? If so, which plan?
takeHomeChat.askPostgrad: Are you also repaying a postgraduate loan?
takeHomeChat.done: You take home about {amount} a month. Close this window to see your payslip, or plan where that money goes next.

pitchChat.open: Build it by chat or voice
pitchChat.title: Your pitch deck, one question at a time
pitchChat.askTagline: What does it do, in one line? This goes under the name on the cover.
pitchChat.askCurrency: Which currency should the deck use?
pitchChat.askProblem: Problem {n} your customers have: name it in two or three words.
pitchChat.askProblemOptional: A third problem? Name it in two or three words, or say “none”.
pitchChat.askProblemDesc: In a sentence, how does “{item}” hurt your customers?
pitchChat.askSolution: How does your company solve these problems? Two or three sentences.
pitchChat.askDiffs: What makes you different? Up to three short points, separated by commas — for example: 10× faster, 50% cheaper.
pitchChat.askTam: How big is the whole market for what you do (TAM), in billions of {sym}?
pitchChat.askSam: And the part of it you can actually serve (SAM), in billions of {sym}?
pitchChat.askSom: And how much of that you can realistically win in the next few years (SOM), in millions of {sym}?
pitchChat.askMarketNote: Anything to add about the market, such as where those figures come from? Or say “none”.
pitchChat.askRevStreams: How do you make money? List your revenue streams, separated by commas.
pitchChat.askPricing: What do you charge? List your prices separated by commas — for example: Starter $49 a month, Growth $199 a month. Or say “none”.
pitchChat.askKpiLabel: Key number {n} that shows your progress — what is it called (customers, monthly revenue…)? Say “none” when you have no more.
pitchChat.askMilestones: What have you achieved so far? List milestones separated by commas, with dates — or say “none”.
pitchChat.askProfitFirst: EBITDA in year 1 — earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation? For a loss, say “loss” or put a minus sign: “loss of 50k”, “-50000”.
pitchChat.askMemberFirst: Who leads the company? Their name, please.
pitchChat.askMember: Team member {n}: their name? Say “none” if that's the whole team.
pitchChat.askMemberBio: One or two lines about {name}: experience, previous roles. Or say “none”.
pitchChat.askFunding: How much are you raising, in {sym}?
pitchChat.askRound: Which kind of round is it?
pitchChat.askAchieve: What will the money let you achieve? List it separated by commas.
pitchChat.askFundsFirst: What will the money go on? Name the first area, such as product or sales.
pitchChat.askFunds: Another area the money will go on? Or say “none”.
pitchChat.askFundsPct: What percentage of the money goes on {item}?
pitchChat.done: Your deck is ready. Download it now, or close this window to check each slide first.
pitchChat.doneFundsOff: Your deck is ready. One thing: your use of funds adds up to {total}%, not 100%. Close this window to fix it on the last slide, or download it as it is.
pitchChat.askWhyNow: Why is now the right time? Name up to three things that changed — technology, regulation, customer habits — separated by commas.
pitchChat.askMarketSource: Where do the market figures come from? A report, a statistics office, your own count — or say “none”.
pitchChat.askCompetitors: What do customers use today instead of you? Name up to four alternatives separated by commas — competitors, spreadsheets, consultants. Or say “none”.
pitchChat.askArpa: On average, how much does one customer pay you a month, in {sym}?
pitchChat.askGrossMargin: What is your gross margin, as a percentage?
pitchChat.askChurn: What percentage of customers leave each month?
pitchChat.askCac: How much does it cost you to win one new customer (sales and marketing spend ÷ new customers), in {sym}?
pitchChat.askAssumptions: What are the two or three assumptions behind those numbers? Separate them with commas — or say “none”.
pitchChat.askRunway: How many months will this money last?
pitchChat.askContact: Which email should investors contact? Or say “none”.
